Abstract—Current heterogeneous systems integrate general-
purpose Central Processing Units (CPUs), Graphics Processing
Units (GPUs), and Neural Processing Units (NPUs). The efficient
use of such systems requires a significant programming effort
to distribute computation and synchronize across devices, which
usually involves using Atomic Memory Operations (AMOs). Arm
recently launched a floating-point Atomic Memory Operations
(FAMOs) extension to perform atomic updates on floating-point
data types specifically.
This work characterizes and models heterogeneous architectures
to understand how floating-point AMOs impact graph, Machine
Learning (ML), and high-performance computing (HPC) work-
loads. Our analysis shows that many AMOs are performed on
floating-point data, which modern systems execute using inefficient
compare-and-swap (CAS) constructs. Therefore, replacing CAS-
based constructs with FAMOs can improve a wide range of
workloads. Moreover, we analyze the trade-offs of executing FAMOs
at different memory hierarchy levels, either in private caches (near)
or remotely in shared caches (far). We have extended the widely
used AMBA CHI protocol to evaluate such FAMO support on a
simulated chiplet-based heterogeneous architecture. While near
FAMOs achieve an average 1.34× speed-up, far FAMOs reach
an average 1.58× speed-up. We conclude that FAMOs can bridge
the gap between CPU architecture and accelerators and enabling
synchronization in key application domains.
I. INTRODUCTION
Heterogeneous architectures are becoming the de facto
standard for executing cutting-edge applications such as gaming,
image processing, and large language models (LLMs). The
latest mobile and laptop systems integrate Central Processing
Units (CPUs), GPUs, and NPUs in their Systems-on-Chip
(SoCs) to accelerate such applications. Heterogeneous systems
also dominate the HPC market, coping 9 out of the 10 most
powerful supercomputers in the world [1]. HPC benefits from
accelerators by solving more complex problems and consuming
less energy [2]. Figure 1 shows an example of a modern HPC
heterogeneous architecture that integrates CPUs, a GPU, and
NPUs.
Software or hardware mechanisms are required to keep
cache coherence and memory consistency across devices in
a heterogeneous system. Heterogeneous Cache Coherence
(HCC) is a design trend that integrates conventional CPUs and
accelerators by relying on traditional multicore cache coherence.
HCC allows fine-grained work distribution between the CPU
and accelerators via barriers and Atomic Memory Operations
(AMOs). However, as complexity in heterogeneous systems
grows, new AMO capabilities are required, such as supporting

floating-point addition), or execution mechanisms (e.g., far AMO
execution). This is the case for Arm’s new Large System Float
Extension (LSFE), which was recently launched to support
floating-point AMOs (FAMOs) [3]. Arm’s FAMOs introduce
five new operations operating with four floating-point data types.
Heterogeneous architectures must incorporate microarchitectural
support to execute FAMOs efficiently.
Most modern systems execute AMOs in the first-level data
cache (near AMOs), which introduces substantial overheads: (1)
serialization, as only one cache can perform an atomic operation
at a time, and (2) traffic since fetching an exclusive copy of the
cache line requires invalidating other copies. Multiple requestors
attempting to acquire an exclusive copy can make the line
ping-pong from one cache to another. Since currently available
general-purpose CPUs do not support FAMOs, programmers
must perform the AMOs using a generic compare-and-swap
(CAS) construct. CAS-based constructs have low throughput
under contention, as the conditional swap can fail due to a write
to the same memory position between the read and the update
operations [4]. Thus, replacing CAS-based constructs with
FAMOs can increase the overall system throughput. However,
FAMOs suffer higher serialization overhead, as the floating-point
operation takes more cycles than regular integer and bitwise
operations. Furthermore, heterogeneous systems require a fast
and efficient cache coherence architecture to avoid harming

parallel efficiency. Integrating FAMOs in such architectures
could compromise the performance of a heterogeneous system.
Therefore, future heterogeneous systems would require efficient
mechanisms to execute workloads using FAMOs.
This work examines several HPC, graph, and ML applications
and finds that a substantial fraction of AMOs are performed on
floating-point data. Although these applications can benefit from
the newly introduced FAMOs, the complexity of floating-point
operations can reduce their scalability, especially on heteroge-
neous architectures where cache coherency is more expensive.
Therefore, we present FLAMA (in Aragonese ”flame”), a Far
Floating-point Atomic Memory Operation Architecture. We
analyze the usage of far AMOs in FLAMA to reduce the data
movement between processing elements. Far AMOs directly
perform the atomic operation at the directory or memory, which
can alleviate cache ping-pong effects. We show that far FAMOs
can significantly improve the efficiency of scatter updates in
terms of latency and memory bandwidth.
In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:
• We analyze a broad set of representative applications (HPC,
Graph Analytics, and Machine Learning) and find that a
significant fraction of atomic updates are performed on
floating-point data.
• We extend gem5 [5] to support an integrated heterogeneous
system enhanced with the FAMOs instructions. Our evalu-
ations show a substantial speed-up in multiple application
domains. FAMOs speed up applications by 58% on average
and up to 3.7× for some atomic-intensive kernels.
• We analyze the hardware cost of supporting FAMOs at
different cache hierarchy levels. In the worst case, FAMOs
have a negligible increase in total chip area by 0.036%,
for a chip with 64 directory slices.
II. BACKGROUND
This section overviews both heterogeneous architectures and
current trends in heterogeneous systems.
A. Heterogeneous Systems
Traditionally, discrete accelerators connect to a host machine
via high-bandwidth, but high-latency interconnects, such as PCI
Express (PCIe). The host and device have different memory
address spaces, so the programmer must explicitly copy data
between the two memory devices.
Such pitfalls pushed towards the tight integration of accel-
erators with conventional CPUs on the same SoC die [6]. On-
die integration offers several benefits: communication through
network-on-chip saves energy and reduces communication
latency, a shared memory address space avoids explicit data
movement and duplication, and reduced communication latency
enables efficient fine-grained data sharing and synchronization.
The resulting system allows programmers to distribute the
computation between devices, each contributing by executing
the code regions on which they are more efficient.
B. Coherent Heterogeneous Architectures
Coherence can be implemented in software, hardware, or
both to make a shared address space transparent to application
programmers. Heterogeneous Cache Coherence (HCC) proposes
maintaining coherence through hardware at the granularity
of cache lines, similar to traditional multicore processors.
Several academic works have proposed different hardware-based
mechanisms to implement HCC in a transparent manner [7]. On
the industry side, multiple vendors have committed to providing
systems supporting HCC, resulting in many standards, such as
Compute Express Link, Nvidia’s NVLink, or Arm’s AMBA 5
CHI. All these standards enable an interface to communicate
with accelerators and CPUs coherently.
However, supporting HCC between CPUs and accelerators
is challenging because each device has distinct memory access
characteristics [8]. For example, GPUs require a much higher
memory bandwidth due to a massively parallel execution model
and exhibit higher spatial and lower temporal locality than
CPU applications. In contrast, CPUs are better suited for
irregular applications than GPUs (conditional code, memory
dependencies, dynamic parallelism, recursion, etc.). A naive
integration of such different computing elements sharing the
last-level cache (LLC) leads to suboptimal cache and memory
bandwidth utilization, load imbalance, or starvation. Despite
current hardware support for HCC, most high-performance
applications still rely on manual data synchronization and
movement between heterogeneous devices.
With the arrival of multi-die or chiplet architectures, the
integration of accelerators has gone one step further. Chip
manufacturers can integrate multiple vendor dies into a single
chip using advanced packaging technology, saving costs and
enabling design reuse. Chiplet designs enable a simple and
intuitive solution to inter-device disturbance. As mentioned,
Figure 1 depicts an example system with HCC that integrates
general-purpose CPUs, a GPU, and NPUs into two chips
connected through a fast interconnection. Each chiplet has a
different NUMA domain, so memory controllers are partitioned
between devices to prevent inter-device disturbance. Each
NUMA domain’s physical memory is partitioned among the
directories of the same chip. Thus, local memory coherence does
not need to traverse the inter-chip connection. Data accesses
across NUMA domains suffer extra latency penalties because
they traverse the inter-chip networks.
C. Hardware Synchronization
Modern CPU instruction set architectures (ISA), such as
x86, POWER9, Armv9, and RISC-V, specify atomic read-
modify-write instructions or Atomic Memory Operations (AMO).
AMOs enable atomic updates to shared data, becoming the
building blocks for implementing high-level synchronization
primitives such as locks, barriers, and lock-free data structures.
Typically, AMOs perform simple operations such as bit-wise
logic (e.g., AND, OR, and XOR), simple integer arithmetic (e.g.,
Addition, Minimum, and Maximum), and data exchange (e.g.,
Swap and Compare-And-Swap). Correspondingly, GPU ISAs
include AMOs to implement simple inter-thread communication.
However, the specific nature of GPU architectures has favored a
broader set of AMOs that cover more complex primitives such as
conditional increment, vector atomic (updates four consecutive
elements), and floating-point operations.

CPU ISAs have recently incorporated more sophisticated
synchronization mechanisms to reduce synchronization over-
heads. For instance, Intel is introducing relaxed AMOs (AAD-
D/AAND/AOR/AXOR) that can be executed remotely and
conditional AMO (CMPccXADD) to perform more complex
operations. Armv9.4 introduced the Large System Extension
128, which supports 16-byte AMO instructions (LDCLRP/LD-
SETP/SWPP/). Finally, Armv9.6 introduced the Large System
Float Extension to perform AMOs in floating-point data.
This trend towards incorporating more specific and complex
AMO primitives must be followed by new microarchitectural
mechanisms to execute them efficiently.
III. MOTIVATION: ANALYZING AMOS IN MODERN
COMPUTING SYSTEMS
System designs are becoming increasingly heterogeneous,
integrating general-purpose CPUs with a wide variety of
accelerators [9]. In this section, we study the role of AMOs when
updating common data structures found in modern applications
across different domains to understand the synchronization
primitives used. We detail the intricacies of hardware and
software techniques when performing shared memory updates.
Reductions are widely used in data analytics applications,
such as image processing, genomic analysis, and particle physics.
Parallel implementations of reductions take advantage of the
commutativity property of increments to divide work among
threads. However, parallel implementations must handle multiple
updates to shared data, as different threads may need to update
the same memory position.
The shared memory programming paradigm allows program-
mers to update shared data through multiple mechanisms:
1) Atomics: AMOs can directly perform single-word and
double-word updates to shared data, implementing an atomic
Read-Modify-Write (RMW) primitive. However, AMOs are
infamous for the overhead and serialization they impose [10].
Thus, most architectures have introduced different consistency
semantics to reduce the cost of AMOs, allowing their reordering.
Atomic-no-return instructions, or AtomicStore, have lower con-
sistency constraints because they perform the RMW operation
without returning the original read value. As a result, many
GPU architectures have spread the use of AMOs and software
tools to perform efficient reductions through AtomicStores.
Most AMO implementations perform the RMW operation on
the private caches (near AMOs). In case of a miss, the private
cache fetches the target cache block with exclusive permissions,
frequently evicting copies of the cache block present on other
private caches. Alternatively, several multicore architectures
implement mechanisms to send the AMO to be performed
where the data resides, typically in the LLC or a memory
controller. Figure 2 illustrates how near and far AMOs work
on a two-chiplet heterogeneous system. One chiplet comprises
general-purpose CPUs (C0 to C8), and the other comprises
accelerators (A0 to A8). Core-6 and Accelerator-1 execute an
AtomicStore (e.g., to signal that they finished their respective
tasks) in a memory position owned by the directory of the
Accelerator-5 tile.
When AtomicStores are executed as near AMOs (2a), Core-6
fetches the cache block into its private cache to perform the
RMW operation. Then, Accelerator-1 also requests the cache
block in exclusivity to the directory. This triggers an invalidation
to the Core-6, and the cache block is transferred to Accelerator-
5’s private cache. In total, four messages had to traverse the
interconnect between both chiplets. When AtomicStores are
executed remotely (far AMOs 2b), Core-6 and Accelerator-1
send their respective Atomic transactions to the directory at the
Accelerator-5 tile where the directory resides. As soon as the
operation finishes, the directory acknowledges both transactions.
In total, two messages are sent across chiplets.
2) Software Techniques: The conventional programming
scheme grants mutual exclusion to ensure that only one thread
updates the shared variable, usually through synchronization
primitives (e.g., locks, barriers, and transactions) or thread-safe
data structures (e.g., lock-free or mutex-guarded algorithms).
However, mutual exclusion approaches incur expensive over-
heads, making them a worse alternative to AMOs.
Privatization is the most popular scheme, as it exploits
commutativity to buffer updates into thread-private storage,
reducing these partial updates later to produce the final value.
Privatization is commonly used to implement reduction variables
efficiently, and it is supported in most parallel languages [11]–
[15]. Privatization works efficiently with scalars and small
arrays. However, privatized data increases the memory footprint
for larger reduction variables, introducing cache pollution

Dynamic privatization schemes [13], [16]–[19] reduce the
space overhead of privatization by just replicating a subset of the
data structures. The main drawbacks of dynamic privatization are
the time overhead required to select privatization candidates and
the increased programming complexity of porting the algorithm.
The state-of-the-art dynamic privatization is PIBOR [17].
To understand the performance tradeoffs of the techniques
above, Figure 3 shows the throughput of a reduction RandomAc-
cess microbenchmark [20] implemented with different schemes:
privatization, PIBOR, near AMOs, and far AMOs in Nvidia’s
Grace Superchip. This microbenchmark measures the throughput
in giga-updates performed per second (GUPs) for different
vector reduction sizes. Privatization is the most performant
approach for small array sizes because it enables concurrent
updates for the same vector element. However, when the array
size increases and reaches the size of the core’s private cache,
privatization performance decreases because the private caches
have a lower hit ratio. Meanwhile, the performance of AMO-
based approaches increases as the number of memory access
conflicts between threads is less likely to happen. Far AMOs
constantly outperform near AMOs for all reduction vector sizes
due to the lower coherence overhead, being the best approach
for vector reduction sizes bigger than 1 MB. The performance of
far AMOs decreases when vector sizes grow over the size of the
LLC until they match the performance of near AMOs. Although
PIBOR outperforms AMO-based approaches for small vector
sizes (lower than 16 KB), PIBOR is never the best-performing
approach. This experiment reveals that AMOs are critical for
large-data-footprint applications in domains such as HPC, graph
analysis, and machine learning.
IV. ATOMICS ON FLOATING POINT DATA
This section analyzes different application domains that
perform atomic updates on floating-point data. Then, we study
how programmers perform AMO over floating-point data in
current systems without support for FAMOs. Finally, we analyze
the recent Arm’s LSFE specification for FAMOs.
A. FAMO Workloads
Atomic floating-point operations are used in applications that
perform reductions as described previously. Thus, we have
analyzed the potential use of FAMOs in a wide range of
applications. We group applications by their domain:
1) HPC: Many HPC applications rely on atomic floating-
point addition. For instance, Partial Differential Equation
(PDE) solvers are the core of various cutting-edge scientific
problems, such as electrodynamics, fluid dynamics, and quantum
mechanics. The most common methods for solving PDEs are
the finite volume, finite element, and spectral element methods,
all of which extensively use floating-point reductions. Other
HPC applications, such as Genomic Analysis, make extensive
use of AMOs [21].
Sparse matrix computations, such as sparse matrix-vector
multiplication (SpMV) or sparse matrix-matrix multiplication
(SpMM), are common in the HPC domain. Both algorithms
perform scatter updates with sparse matrices in Compressed
Sparse Column (CSC) or Coordinate list (COO) storage formats,
relying on floating-point reductions.
2) Machine Learning and Large Language Models: Several
Machine Learning kernels, such as cost function (Negative
log-likelihood loss and connection temporal classification loss)
and gradient computation (Adaptive Pooling, Padding, and Up-
Sample gradients), use atomic floating-point RMW in their
parallel versions. Furthermore, some machine learning models
use sparse matrices to reduce the memory footprint of deep
learning models with billions of parameters [22].
3) Graph Analytics: Many graph analytics applications
iterate over large sets of nodes, requiring updates on many
of them. Those updates are often done concurrently, requiring
atomic operations. Graph analysis frameworks compute using
different types of atomic floating-point RMW, such as minimum,
maximum, and addition.
B. FAMOs in Modern Systems
Although Arm has released the FAMOs specification, no
modern CPU provides any instructions to support atomic
floating-point addition. As a replacement, programmers can
use CAS instructions to implement the same functionality.
Listing 1 implements a double precision floating point Atomic
Fetch&Add in C language (CAS built-in). However, the CAS
built-in introduces a higher serialization overhead than regular
AMOs and far-AMOs, as CAS instructions might not succeed.
The built-in has to iterate on a while loop that performs
CAS instructions because another thread update can happen
between the atomic_load and the CAS or between two CAS
operations. This behavior introduces a substantial overhead when
multiple threads try to update the same memory position.
Listing 1: Floating Point Atomic Fetch&Add Builtin
double fetch_and_add_double(double* ptr, double
inc)
{
double oldValue = atomic_load(ptr);
double newValue;
do {
newValue = oldValue + inc;
} while (!atomic_compare_exchange(ptr, &(oldValue),
newValue));
return oldValue;
}


To avoid the CAS built-in, programmers can use other soft-
ware techniques, such as privatization or delegation. However,
as applications grow in complexity, these techniques become
unfeasible. For instance, to implement privatization in graph
analytics applications, the programmer must replicate the graph
data structure to store thread-local updates and compute the
global reduction later.
Additionally, CAS operations work better when performed
in the private levels of the cache hierarchy [23]. For a failed
far CAS, the latest copy of the data must be returned to the
processing element, which recomputes the new value and issues
a new far CAS operation. This round-trip latency introduces
significant overheads and increases the likelihood the far CAS
will fail again under high contention.
C. FAMOs and FLAMA
As we have shown, FAMOs are relevant in multiple domain-
specific applications. Arm has released five atomic floating-
point operations to ease the synchronization overheads in such
applications: addition, maximum, minimum, maximum-number,
and minimum-number. Architects implementing these FAMOs
must take care of several technical details of the ISA. New
instructions must respect the precision standard, the exception
model, and the consistency model. In this section, we cover the
technical details to implement FAMOs using the Far Floating-
point Atomic Memory Operation Architecture (FLAMA, in
Aragonese ”flame”).
1) Floating Point Standard: Most systems implement floating-
point data types following the IEEE 754 Standard. This standard
supports half (16-bit), single (32-bit), and double (64-bit)
precision floating-point data types. However, other standards
with fewer mantissa bits (bfloat16) or lower range (FP8) have
emerged to accelerate deep learning workloads. Arm’s FAMOs
support half, single, double, and bfloat16 data types.
2) Floating Point Status: Floating point systems that follow
the IEEE 754 standard require tracking the system’s config-
uration (rounding configuration and not-a-number treatment)
and the status of past floating point instructions (flags and
exceptions). In Arm, the Floating Point Control Register (FPCR)
and the Floating-point Status Register (FPSR) are read and
written on every floating-point operation to keep track of this
information.
However, vendors cannot afford to send both registers back
and forth to the directory for far AMOs because doing so
would harden their consistency constraints. To enable fast and
efficient floating-point AMOs in the directory, Arm simplifies
the execution and avoids reading or writing FPSR and FPCR.
Arm’s FAMOs cannot cause floating-point exceptions as they
disable FPSR exception bits and disallow trapping on them.
FAMOs also disable alternative behaviors and only generate
not-a-number de-normalized numbers.
3) Consistency: Since AMOs are read and write instructions,
their interaction with the consistency model is complex and
may impose significant serialization overhead in the memory
hierarchy. Some architectures have adopted non-return instruc-
tions to alleviate the consistency constraints at the cost of lower
functionality. Arm’s FAMOs support both return and non-return

4) Hardware Cost: Modern high-performance CPUs would
require minimal changes to current microarchitectures, as they
already support other AMOs. The main hardware feature
required by FAMOs is a floating-point functional unit (FPU)
that performs the arithmetic addition for each data type. In
the case of near AMOs, the operation is performed either in
the Load-Store-Queue or the first-level data cache. Thus, the
existing core’s FPU can be used for near FAMOs. For far
FAMOs that can be executed in the LLC, the directory, or
the memory controller, a new FPU has to be included in each
AMO-capable component. For example, for a system with 64
distributed directories, we would need at least 64 FPUs. We
estimate the area overheads of these changes in Section V-C.
V. EVALUATION
A. Experimental Methodology
Simulation Infrastructure: We have used the gem5 (v22.0.0)
performance simulator [5] to evaluate the proposed infrastructure.
Gem5 includes cycle-approximate models of various system
components, including cores, a cache hierarchy with a detailed
mesh-based network-on-chip, and memory controllers. We use
the Arm ISA and Ruby to model the AMBA 5 CHI coherence
protocol in a Network-on-Chip with mesh topology. We perform
full-system simulations using Ubuntu 22.04 with Linux Kernel
5.4.65.
Baseline System: We aim to simulate a heterogeneous multi-
chip system with two chiplets connected with a high-bandwidth,
memory-coherent interconnect. However, using the GPU Full
System (GPUFS) is unfeasible due to CPU ISA and coherence

Therefore, we model an asymmetric CPU-only heterogeneous
system with two chiplets to mimic the targeted system. One
chip integrates 16 Armv9 out-of-order cores with small vector
throughput but high Instruction Level Parallelism for general-
purpose workloads (general-purpose partition). The second chip
integrates 40 in-order cores with long vector units for massively
data-parallel codes (vector partition). All cores run at 3 GHz,
while the NoC and the LLC run at 2 GHz. The peak throughput
of the general-purpose partition is 48 GFLOPs (one core can
perform 16 FLOP/cycle), and for the vector partition is 192
GFLOPs (64 FLOP/cycle/core). Both chips are interconnected
through a high bandwidth interconnect serving up to 450 GB/s in
each direction. All the microarchitectural details are summarized
in Table I. We have extended the existing Arm ISA and CHI
protocol implementation to support FAMO instructions.
Workloads: We use a representative set of parallel applications
from the three main domains that can take advantage of FAMOs:
• HPC: We have evaluated classic scientific applications such
as Fluidanimate from the PARSEC benchmark suite [24],
miniFE application from the Sandia National Laborato-
ries [27], and Particle-in-Cell from the UCLA PICKSC
group [28].
• Graph Analytics: Galois [29] is a graph analytics frame-
work that contains classic graph analysis algorithms. We
have selected three graph kernels: PageRank, Leiden-
Clustering, and Louvain-Clustering.
• Sparse Data Kernels: The Deep Graph Library [30] (DGL)
is a sparse deep learning library that works with Pytorch
and TensorFlow. We have used the DGL’s SPMV and
SPMM kernels for CSC and COO matrix formats.
We have vectorized (automatically, using directives, or
manually) all benchmarks.
Synthesis and Physical Design Environment: The area analysis
of a floating-point arithmetic unit was performed using the
Global-Foundries 22nm FD-SOI technology node. Our physical
design targets post-routing clock timing of 2 GHz. We used the
Cadence Genus tool v19.11 for the logical synthesis and the
Cadence Innovus tool v19.11 for the place-and-route.
B. Evaluation of Floating-Point AMOs
We evaluate three different alternatives to perform floating
point AMOs: using the CAS builtin (CAS), executing FAMOs in
the L1 Data cache (near FAMO), and executing the FAMOs in
the LLC (far FAMO). We omitted privatization in our analysis,
as some HPC and Graph benchmarks would require complex
code modifications and face out-of-memory issues.
1) Performance Comparison: Figure 4 shows the relative
speed-up of the three different versions using all the cores in
both partitions, normalized with respect to CAS Builtin. We
can observe that simply replacing CAS builtins with FAMOs,
either executing at the L1D or the LLC, leads to substantial
performance improvements (up to 3.7× in VCO). First, the
CAS builtin iterates on a while loop that depends on the
CAS’s success. Since the CAS success has no predictable
pattern, we observe many branch prediction misses that reduce
when introducing FAMOs (e.g., from 15% to 1.4% on VCO).
Furthermore, the CAS builtin introduces a harmful memory
dependency (between atomic load/CAS and CAS/CAS) that
reduces the available ILP of the code. For instance, the
number of memory order violations decreases by 99% on VCO
when replacing CAS builtin with FAMOs. The performance
improvement of FAMOs is lower in applications like FLU,
MFE, and PIC. AMOs represent a residual weight in the total
instruction mix in these applications. On average, near FAMOs
perform 1.34× faster than the CAS builtin.
When the FAMOs are executed at the LLC rather than
the L1D, we can observe additional speed-ups in VCS, VCO,
and MCO. However, MFE and PIC experience performance
degradation when FAMOs are executed at the LLC. The intrinsic
data access pattern of each benchmark explains this application-
dependent behavior. Some applications have a data reuse pattern
that favors near FAMO execution over far FAMO execution.
Programmers can profile applications to predict the performance
outcome of applying near or far FAMOs. On average, far FAMOs
perform 1.58× faster than the CAS builtin, and 1.17× faster
than executing FAMOs in the L1D.
2) Scalability Comparison: We have performed a strong
scalability analysis to understand how benchmarks perform
for non-collaborative configurations (i.e., only using general-
purpose or vector partition) with respect to a collaborative
configuration (i.g., using both general-purpose and vector parti-
tions). We have evaluated five non-collaborative configurations
that only use the general-purpose partition (denoted with G-
#ofthreads), one non-collaborative configuration that uses the
vector partition (V-40), and one collaborative configuration that
uses all available threads (G-16-V-40). Figure 5 shows the strong
analysis for MCO kernel (5a) and for PIC application (5b). Both
figures present the normalized execution time with respect to
single-thread general-purpose partition performance (G-1) on a
logarithmic scale.
The scalability of MCO is almost linear for the general-
purpose partition CPUs. All 16 out-of-order CPUs from the
general-purpose partition nearly match the vector partition per-
formance using 40 PEs. Thanks to its higher vector throughput,
vector partitions have higher floating-point peak performance,
but the sparse nature of MCO hinders this performance. This
configuration already saturates the cache hierarchy with a miss
rate of 92% in the L2 and a 61% in the LLC. Thus, the

C. Hardware Cost
To measure the hardware overhead of FAMOs, we have
synthesized an unoptimized arithmetic FPU with fused multiply-
add capabilities (IEEE 754 for 64, 32, and 16 bits). This module
occupies 0.013139 mm2 in a 22nm process, targeting 2 GHz. To
consider the overall impact on a full system, we must consider
the number of directory slices in the chip. For instance, the
AWS Graviton 2 (with far AMO capabilities) has 64 directory
slices and an estimated die size of 456.96mm2 in a 7nm process.
Assuming a conservative logic density scaling factor of 5× from
a 22nm to a 7nm process, including an FPU per directory slice
would increase the total chip area by only 0.036%. Note that this
area could be optimized further by removing the multiplication
capabilities, increasing the unit’s latency, or sharing an FPU
across two or more directory slices.
VI. RELATED WORK
Academic literature has observed that atomic updates to
shared data are inefficient in conventional cache hierarchies
and has profusely explored hardware and software techniques
to enhance them.
1) Atomic Memory Operations: Other academic works in
the past have explored different AMO semantics to speed up
applications. Some works propose vector atomics that perform
multiple atomic operations [31], [32].
2) Accelerators: Some works have proposed hardware-
accelerated designs that speed up atomically intensive applica-
tions. Tascade [33] proposes an SRAM-based accelerator for
graph analysis that uses a delegation scheme to partition graph
workloads. Tascade architecture uses a hardware reduction tree
to minimize the cost of atomic updates. Nevertheless, these
accelerators do not improve the interaction between CPUs and
accelerators.
3) Coalescing Optimizaitons: Several works exploit data
commutativity to coalesce atomic updates [34]–[36]. These
approaches usually perform changes in the coherence protocol
or the consistency model.
VII. CONCLUSIONS
Heterogeneous integrated systems are here to stay. Future
system designs will integrate more and more accelerators.
In this paper, we analyze and evaluate the performance of
heterogeneous systems composed of general-purpose CPUs and
accelerators. Optimizing the synchronization between devices is
critical to maximizing the system’s performance. Furthermore,
we analyze different applications and find that floating-point
addition is a relevant synchronization primitive in many domains.
We then analyze the Large System Float Extension released
by Arm to support floating-point atomics. We model a hetero-
geneous integrated system in gem5 and demonstrate that near
and far FAMOs reduce serialization costs and execution time.

Abstract: Current heterogeneous systems integrate general- purpose Central Processing Units (CPUs), Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), and Neural Processing Units (NPUs). The efficient use of such systems requires a significant programming effort to distribute computation and synchronize across devices, which usually involves using Atomic Memory Operations (AMOs). Arm recently launched a floating-point Atomic Memory Operations (FAMOs) extension to perform atomic updates on floating-point data types specifically. This work characterizes and models heterogeneous architectures to understand how floating-point AMOs impact graph, Machine Learning (ML), and high-performance computing (HPC) work- loads. Our analysis shows that many AMOs are performed on floating-point data, which modern systems execute using inefficient compare-and-swap (CAS) constructs. Therefore, replacing CAS- based constructs with FAMOs can improve a wide range of workloads. Moreover, we analyze the trade-offs of executing FAMOs at different memory hierarchy levels, either in private caches (near) or remotely in shared caches (far). We have extended the widely used AMBA CHI protocol to evaluate such FAMO support on a simulated chiplet-based heterogeneous architecture. While near FAMOs achieve an average 1.34× speed-up, far FAMOs reach an average 1.58× speed-up. We conclude that FAMOs can bridge the gap between CPU architecture and accelerators and enabling synchronization in key application domains.
